title: Dagesh, gutturals, and shin and sin

objectives.can: Tell dagesh lene from dagesh forte, read the six begadkefat letters, and say how the gutturals behave.

explanation.summary: A dot inside a Hebrew letter can mean two different things, and a few letters behave in their own way. Learning when a dot makes a hard sound, when it doubles a letter, and how the guttural letters change the vowels near them lets you read most pointed words correctly.

sections.heading: The dot inside a letter: dagesh
body: The Masoretes wrote a dot in a letter and called it a dagesh. It has two quite different jobs, and one dot looks the same as the other. The dagesh lene (the 'light' dagesh) belongs to six letters only and makes them hard. The dagesh forte (the 'strong' dagesh) doubles a letter, as though it were written twice.

A dagesh in any letter other than ב ג ד כ פ ת is always a dagesh forte. A dagesh in one of those six letters is a lene if no vowel sound comes just before it, and a forte if a vowel does. In the traditional rule: at the beginning of a word, or after a silent shewa, it is a lene. Right after a vowel it is a forte. (A letter at the beginning of a word can also lose its dagesh lene when the word before it ends in a vowel and runs on into it; the pointing in the verses you read shows each case.)

sections.heading: The six begadkefat letters
body: The six letters are ב ג ד כ פ ת, which teachers remember as 'begadkefat' (the letters of the mnemonic). With a dagesh lene they have a hard sound. Without one, after a vowel, they are soft. In Modern Hebrew the difference is audible for three of them: ב is 'b' or 'v', כ is 'k' or 'kh', and פ is 'p' or 'f'.

Descriptions of the old reading tradition say that ג ד ת also had a soft sound. These soft sounds are a reconstruction and Modern Hebrew has lost them; you will see them in the table as the 'Tiberian' column. Whichever reading you use, the spelling is the same.

sections.heading: Dagesh forte and mappiq
body: A dagesh forte shows that a letter is doubled, like the double letters of Italian. It is written after the article, so that the first letter of the noun is doubled: the shin of הַשָּׁמַיִם, 'the heavens'. It is written inside many verb stems, as the second י of וַיַּבְדֵּל.
A dot in a final ה is a third thing, called a mappiq. It shows that the ה is a real consonant and is pronounced, not a silent vowel letter. In כֹּחָהּ, 'her strength', the final ה is pronounced 'ha'.

sections.heading: The gutturals
body: Four letters are made in the throat: א ה ח ע. A fifth letter, ר, shares some of their behaviour. Their rules are habits rather than laws, and the pointing shows the habits.

A guttural does not take a dagesh forte. When a letter would be doubled and it is a guttural, the vowel before it is often lengthened instead, as in הָאָרֶץ, 'the earth', where the article has a qamets before א (where ordinary letters would take a patah and a dagesh).

A guttural prefers a-class vowels and, where another letter would have a silent or a vocal shewa, a guttural often takes a composite shewa: a very short vowel, the hatef segol of אֱלֹהִים or the hatef patah of הָאֲדָמָה.

At the end of a word, a ח or ע after a vowel that is not a-class is pronounced with a very short a sounding before it, called a furtive patah. רוּחַ, 'wind, spirit', is read 'ru-akh', with the a before the kh, though in writing the patah is below the ח.

sections.heading: Shin and sin
body: ש is two letters with one shape, told apart by a dot. A dot over the right side, שׁ, is shin, 'sh'. A dot over the left side, שׂ, is sin, 's'. Both letters are dotted in every pointed word. You will meet them at once: בְּרֵאשִׁית has a shin and וַיַּעַשׂ has a sin.

misunderstandings: A dot in a begadkefat letter is not always a lene. If a vowel stands right before it, it is a dagesh forte and the letter is doubled.
A dot in any letter outside the six is always a forte. It can never be a lene.
The gutturals usually refuse a dagesh forte, but they do not all behave in the same way: ה and ח and ע show their habits somewhat differently, and ר is only partly like them.
A furtive patah is not silent. It is pronounced, but before the guttural, although it is written under it.
Shin and sin are not variant pronunciations of one letter. The dot makes them two distinct letters.

deeper.heading: Compensatory lengthening
body: When a guttural or ר refuses a dagesh forte, the vowel before it is sometimes lengthened to make up for the lost doubling, so the article that is הַ before most letters is הָ before א and ר. This is called compensatory lengthening. Before ה ח ע, grammarians describe the article as sometimes keeping patah and sometimes becoming הֶ or הָ, depending on the vowel of the following syllable.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: IN THE beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בְּרֵאשִׁית and בָּרָא begin with ב and a dagesh lene: nothing comes before the letter in the word, so it is hard, 'b'. The ש of בְּרֵאשִׁית has its dot on the right: it is shin. In הַשָּׁמַיִם the dot inside the ש is a dagesh forte, because ש is not one of the six letters; the shin is doubled after the article.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God saw the light, that it was good; and God divided the light from the darkness.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: הָאוֹר has a qamets under the article's ה because א cannot be doubled: the vowel is lengthened instead. In וַיַּבְדֵּל the ב has no dagesh, because the patah of the doubled י stands right before it, so it is soft; the ד has a dagesh lene, because it follows the silent shewa of the ב and no vowel stands right before it. The second י has a dagesh forte. In הַחֹשֶׁךְ the ח is a guttural and takes no dagesh after the article.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: Now the earth was unformed and void, and darkness was upon the face of the deep; and the spirit of God hovered over the face of the waters.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וְרוּחַ ends in ח, after the long vowel u (the ו with a dot). The patah below the ח is a furtive patah, pronounced before the ח: 'ru-akh'. In אֱלֹהִים the א, a guttural, takes a hatef segol, a very short e, instead of a plain shewa.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And God made the firmament, and divided the waters which were under the firmament from the waters which were above the firmament; and it was so.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The last letter of וַיַּעַשׂ has its dot on the left: it is sin, sounded s. The second י has a dagesh forte. הָרָקִיעַ ends in ע after a long vowel, so the patah under it is a furtive patah, pronounced before the ע; and the article has a qamets before ר, which refuses a dagesh forte.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: When thou tillest the ground, it shall not henceforth yield unto thee her strength; a fugitive and a wanderer shalt thou be in the earth.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: In כֹּחָהּ the first letter has a dagesh lene (the word begins with it). The final ה has a dot, a mappiq: it is a consonant, 'ha', and the word means 'her strength', with the ending that is the pronoun 'her'.
